questions.question: Which three financial statements form the core set for any business?

options.text: Sales report, HR report, and tax return
Profit and Loss statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow statement
Budget, Forecast, and Variance report
Payroll register, Inventory list, and Fixed Asset schedule

questions.explanation: The three core financial statements are: P&L (income statement) — profitability over a period; Balance Sheet — assets and liabilities at a point in time; Cash Flow — cash movements.

questions.question: Gross Profit is calculated as:

options.text: Total Revenue minus Operating Expenses
Total Revenue minus Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)
Total Revenue minus Taxes
Net Profit plus Depreciation

questions.explanation: Gross Profit = Revenue - COGS. It reflects the profit from core business activities before deducting operating expenses like salaries, rent, and marketing.

questions.question: The fundamental accounting equation underlying every balance sheet is:

options.text: Revenue - Expenses = Profit
Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' Equity
Cash In - Cash Out = Net Cash Flow
Assets - Liabilities = Revenue

questions.explanation: The accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity is always true by definition. It ensures the balance sheet always balances — every asset is funded either by debt or equity.

questions.question: Why can a profitable company still run out of cash?

options.text: Because revenue is always equal to cash received
Because profit is an accounting concept that does not always reflect actual cash timing
Because profitable companies have no expenses
This situation cannot occur in practice

questions.explanation: Profit is accrual-based: a company records revenue when earned, not when cash is received. Customers may pay late, inventory requires upfront cash, and capex precedes revenue — creating cash gaps despite profitability.

questions.question: What is 'runway' in startup finance terminology?

options.text: The physical office space available to the team
The number of months a startup can operate at current burn rate before running out of cash
The growth rate of the startup in the last quarter
The amount of revenue generated per employee

questions.explanation: Runway = Cash Balance / Monthly Burn Rate. It tells founders how much time they have to achieve milestones before needing additional funding.

questions.question: What does it mean when a business has a Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) to Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) ratio of less than 1?

options.text: The business is highly profitable and growing efficiently
The business loses money on each customer and the model is unsustainable
The business is breaking even on customer acquisition
The ratio has no meaningful interpretation

questions.explanation: CLV/CAC < 1 means the company spends more acquiring each customer than it will ever recover from them — a fundamental unit economics problem that makes the business unsustainable.

questions.question: EBITDA stands for:

options.text: Earnings Before Income Tax and Depreciation Adjustments
Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortisation
Enterprise Budget Including Total Debt Allocation
Equity, Business Income, Tax Deductions, and Allowances

questions.explanation: EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortisation) is used as a proxy for operating cash generation and is widely used in startup and M&A valuations.

questions.question: When reading a startup's financial statements, which is the most critical warning sign for investors?

options.text: High gross margins
Negative operating cash flow with no clear path to cash breakeven
Rapidly growing revenue
Low debt-to-equity ratio

questions.explanation: Persistent negative operating cash flow without a credible path to breakeven signals that the business cannot sustain itself without continuous external capital, posing an existential risk.
